source.title_on_document: When AI Joins the Brainstorm: Impacts of Generative Language Models on Collaborative Divergent Thinking

supplement.where: No supplementary material or appendix is identified in the document. On p. 4, Intervention Design, the authors refer to La Scala et al. (2025a) and La Scala et al. (2025b) for additional system details and screenshots.
supplement.holds: No statistics are said to be located in an external supplement. References occupy pp. 14–17; there is no appendix in this PDF.

paper_design_summary: In a university course, student project groups were assigned to a factorial experiment combining live or round-based idea sharing with the presence or absence of a GPT-4o AI peer (pp. 4–5, Study design and Workshop Session). Students generated short ideas for their digital-innovation projects while AI-treated groups received automatically generated ideas; the authors scored participants' fluency and their ideas' elaboration and originality (pp. 6–8). The same dataset also supplied an AI-generated versus human-generated originality comparison and analyses of collaboration and user experience, rather than separate experiments (pp. 8–10).

studies.label: Course-based group ideation: live versus rounds crossed with AI peer versus no AI peer

assignment.what_was_assigned: Student project groups were assigned to Live, Rounds, Live AI, or Rounds AI, crossing collaboration modality with AI-peer presence. Groups were self-organized before condition assignment, and each condition met in a separate classroom. The paper calls the experiment randomized but does not describe the randomization procedure or give allocation counts (pp. 1, 4–5).
assignment.quote: We conducted a randomized controlled experiment (N=96) with four conditions, varying two factors: the structure of idea sharing (live vs. round-based), and the presence of an AI peer generating ideas using a Generative Language Model.
assignment.locator: p. 1, Abstract; p. 4, Study design and Participants; p. 5, Workshop Session (groups assigned to the four conditions)

arms.name: Live
arms.description: Live collaboration without an AI peer: students' ideas were shared in real time on the same collaborative ideation board (pp. 4–5).

arms.name: Rounds
arms.description: Round-based collaboration without an AI peer: students saw the group's ideas from preceding rounds; the first round had no pre-existing ideas (pp. 4–5).

arms.name: Live AI
arms.description: Live collaboration with a GPT-4o AI peer that automatically submitted one idea whenever users had submitted three ideas. AI-generated ideas were identified as such (pp. 4–5).

arms.name: Rounds AI
arms.description: Round-based collaboration with a GPT-4o AI peer generating two ideas per round. Ideas were shared between rounds, and AI-generated contributions were identified as such (pp. 4–5).

participants.exclusions: The course involved 108 students; 96 consented to research. Nonconsenting students still joined the workshop but contributed no collected research data (p. 4, Participants). No further participant-level exclusions or outcome-specific participant counts are stated. For output analyses, contributions rated 1 for relevance by either rater and non-idea contributions were filtered, leaving 582 ideas (p. 6); p. 7 reports 680 ideas initially rated, and p. 8 identifies 156 AI and 426 human ideas in the retained pool. The 96 entered as analyzed is the paper's overall experimental sample, supported by the conclusion and the statement that all participants were pooled (p. 14), not an arm-specific or outcome-specific analysis count. The paper separately reports 99 questionnaire responses and 63 responses retained for qualitative analysis (p. 10); this discrepancy is unexplained.
participants.who: Bachelor-level students taking an information systems design course, enrolled in economics, data science, or sports and economics programs. They worked in self-organized project groups of up to five; the paper reports 23 groups (p. 4, Participants; p. 14, Conclusion).
participants.country: Switzerland (p. 14, Limitations: one class at a Swiss university)
participants.quote: Our experiment with 96 students across 23 groups revealed several key contributions.
participants.locator: p. 1, Abstract (N=96); p. 4, Participants (108 course students, 96 consenting); p. 14, Limitations (all participants pooled; Swiss university) and Conclusion (96 students across 23 groups)

ai_tool.name_model: OpenAI GPT-4o (p. 4, Intervention Design; p. 16, OpenAI software reference)
ai_tool.how_used: An AI peer embedded in the Graasp collaborative ideation board automatically generated initial ideas from a prompt containing the group's problem statement, other participants' ideas, and instructions to generate a new idea. Its ideas were labeled AI-generated. It could not build on an existing idea. Throughput was two ideas per round in Rounds AI and one idea per three user submissions in Live AI (p. 4, Intervention Design).

task.description: Generate short, anonymous ideas, limited to 200 characters, proposing solutions to a group-defined problem for a digital innovation prototype aligned with a United Nations Sustainable Development Goal. Students could append contributions to peers' ideas. This was the ideation stage of their ongoing coursework, not an Alternative Uses Task (pp. 4–5).
task.duration: The workshop was described as two hours, with a nominal 15-minute ideation phase followed by five minutes of voting (p. 5, Workshop Session). Actual ideation durations varied; fluency was normalized to ideas per 15 minutes (pp. 6–7).

outcomes.name: Originality of human-generated ideas with versus without an AI peer
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: The paper documents both OCSAI automated originality scoring and two human raters using a seven-point originality scale, with originality normalized to 0–1. It reports human-rater agreement r = .45, p < .001; each rater versus OCSAI r = .57 and r = .62, both p < .001; and mean human score versus OCSAI r = .70, p < .001 (pp. 7–8, Ideas' Originality; Fig. 3). These are validation variants of the same originality construct. The text does not explicitly identify whether the subsequent condition-effect model uses OCSAI, mean human ratings, or a combined score, so the single-valued measure field is null rather than choosing an unconfirmed source. Human-generated ideas were analyzed at the idea level with a normal Bayesian model (p. 8, equation 4); the retained human-idea pool is N = 426, without arm-specific model Ns (p. 8).

contrasts.reported: d_agent = -0.17 (HDI 94%: [-0.44, 0.10]). The paper describes no significant effect; the negative point estimate has an interval spanning zero. The paper labels this an effect size but does not specify its standardizer.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Ideas' Originality, paragraph following equation (4)

contrasts.reported: d_agent = -0.24 (HDI 94%: [-0.51, 0.01]). The authors interpret this as slightly less original ideas with an AI peer; the printed interval nevertheless includes zero. The paper labels this an effect size but does not specify its standardizer.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Ideas' Originality, paragraph following equation (4)

outcomes.name: Participant creative fluency: number of ideas per 15 minutes
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Each participant's number of ideas was divided by their group's activity duration and multiplied by 15 minutes (p. 7, equation 1). The authors fitted a negative-binomial Bayesian model at participant level (pp. 6–7, equation 2); Fig. 1 shows distributions by AI presence within each collaboration mode. No arm-level participant counts or numeric means/SDs are given. The ancillary correlation of group time with idea count is retained here as a related analysis, not a separate outcome: rounds Pearson (N = 10): r(8) = 0.94, p < 0.001; live Pearson (N = 9): r(7) = -0.65, p = 0.059 (p. 6, Fig. 2 and accompanying paragraph). These N values are groups, not people.

contrasts.reported: d_agent = -0.61 (HDI 94%: [-1.22, -0.07]) in live collaboration. The paper labels this an effect size but does not specify its standardizer.
contrasts.locator: p. 7, Participant's Creative Fluency, paragraph following equation (2); p. 6, Fig. 1

contrasts.reported: d_collaboration = -0.79 (HDI 94%: [-1.39, -0.26]) without any AI peer. This is a collaboration-modality contrast among the no-AI arms, retained for completeness; it is not an AI-assistance estimate.

outcomes.name: Elaboration of participants' ideas: word count after stopword removal
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Deterministic elaboration score: the number of words in an idea after removing stopwords with NLTK and its stopword corpus (p. 7, Participants Elaboration). The automated_score category here denotes an automated word-count score, not an LLM judge. A normal Bayesian model was fitted at idea level (pp. 6–7, equation 3). The exact elaboration-model observation count is not stated.

contrasts.reported: d_agent = 0.05, HDI 94%: [-0.19, 0.3]. The paper labels this an effect size but does not specify its standardizer.
contrasts.locator: p. 7, Participants Elaboration, paragraph following equation (3)
p. 7, Participants Elaboration, paragraph following equation (3)

outcomes.name: Originality of AI-generated versus human-generated ideas in the same experiment
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Comparison by idea author, using the same retained pool rather than an independent study. Originality was normalized to 0–1; OCSAI and two human raters are described, but the particular score source for the reported author-type comparison is not explicitly identified (pp. 7–8; see S1-O1). The human pool includes ideas from the experiment's conditions and is not described as exclusively unaided. This comparison therefore does not identify the effect of giving people AI assistance.

contrasts.reported: AI-generated ideas: mean = 0.64, median = 0.64, SD = 0.12, N = 156; human-generated ideas: mean = 0.44, median = 0.44, SD = 0.16, N = 426. One-sided Mann-Whitney U = 56620, p < .001. All Ns here count ideas, not people. Shapiro-Wilk checks: W_AI = 0.98, p = .014; W_hum = 0.99, p = 0.001.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Ideas' Originality, paragraph preceding equation (4), and Fig. 4

eligibility.reason: The paper explicitly describes a randomized experiment (p. 1, Abstract; p. 4, Study design) and assigns student project groups to AI-peer presence/absence crossed with live/round-based sharing during ordinary coursework (p. 5, Workshop Session), supporting field_rct with team assignment. Its reported experimental research sample is 96 consenting students; the conclusion repeats 96 students across 23 groups and the limitations state that all participants were pooled (p. 4, Participants; p. 14, Limitations and Conclusion). The course enrollment of 108 and idea counts are not substituted for people. Fluency, elaboration, and originality are computed or rated from produced output (pp. 6–8), with AI available in treated groups while that output was produced (pp. 4–5). Missing arm counts, an unexplained questionnaire count, and lack of adjustment for group assignment constrain extraction and pooling, but do not change the paper's reported eligibility. The embedded author-type comparison is coded separately as an ai_vs_human contrast, not as the main design or a second study.

one_line_finding: An AI peer reduced fluency during live collaboration (d_agent = -0.61, 94% HDI [-1.22, -0.07], p. 7), while originality point estimates were negative but both intervals included zero (live -0.17 [-0.44, 0.10]; rounds -0.24 [-0.51, 0.01], p. 8).
open_questions: What were the actual numbers assigned and analyzed in each of the four arms, and the outcome-specific numbers of people? The paper gives 96 consenting/experimental students (pp. 1, 4, 14), but not an allocation or participant-flow table.

How do the 99 questionnaire responses (p. 10) relate to the 96 consenting students (p. 4), and why does the group-level duration analysis use N = 9 live and N = 10 rounds groups (p. 6) when the experiment is described as 23 groups (pp. 4, 14)?

Which originality score, OCSAI, mean human ratings, or a combination, was used for the reported Bayesian condition effects and AI-versus-human comparison? Both methods and their correlations are described, but the model's score source is not explicit (pp. 7–8).

What denominator defines d_agent and d_collaboration, and can uncertainty accounting for group assignment and repeated ideas within participants be obtained? The paper provides 94% HDIs but no effect-size formula or group-adjusted analysis (pp. 5–8, 14).
Does this sample overlap with any related project paper cited on p. 4? The current PDF does not state participant reuse.
notes: Read the complete markdown conversion and checked the PDF's 17 pages, including all figures, the table, and the references; no appendix is included. PDF and printed page numbers coincide. Outcome inventory: Fig. 1 reports participant fluency; Fig. 2 reports group activity time versus idea count (p. 6); elaboration is in the text and equation (3) (p. 7); Figs. 3–4 and the surrounding text report originality, agreement between scoring methods, and the AI-versus-human originality comparison (pp. 7–8); Figs. 5–6 report direct descendants/co-construction of ideas (pp. 8–9); Fig. 7 reports hedonic and pragmatic user-experience scores (pp. 9–10); Table 1 reports qualitative themes about perceived application impact (pp. 10–12). Relevance was also rated on output but used as an exclusion screen, without a reported AI-condition relevance outcome (pp. 6–7). The outcomes array contains three AI-assistance output outcomes and a separately labeled author-type originality comparison from the same study. The ancillary collaboration result is retained here because only a pooled round-versus-live contrast, not an AI-assistance contrast, is reported: direct descendants per idea, live mean = 0.13, SD = 0.41, n_live = 356; rounds mean = 0.43, SD = 0.72, n_round = 324; one-sided Mann-Whitney U = 45686.5, p < .001; descendant count versus originality r = -.09, p = 0.03, N = 582 (p. 9). Those n values count ideas; direct descendants measure explicit building on another idea, not similarity/diversity across people's outputs. UEQ-S and qualitative perceptions are not scores on creative output and are not included in the outcomes array; p. 10 reports 99 questionnaire responses and 63 retained for qualitative analysis. No across-people similarity/diversity measure, unassisted post-AI creative task, or scored voting outcome is reported. The sample count of 96 is the overall experimental sample stated by the authors; no individual-arm or outcome-specific participant count is recoverable, and a count specifically at random assignment is not given. On p. 6 the authors explicitly analyze fluency at individual level and elaboration/originality at idea level because the number of groups was insufficient for their group-level or multilevel modeling; p. 14 repeats this limitation. Thus the reported precision does not account for the team assignment, and idea-level precision also does not account for multiple ideas per person. Keep the printed effects but do not treat these intervals as cluster-adjusted precision for pooling. confidence_interval in statistics_available represents the printed 94% Bayesian highest-density interval, not a 95% frequentist confidence interval; standardized_effect identifies the printed d labels, whose standardizer is not supplied. No effect size, standard error, interval, count, or graph value was calculated. Originality directions are coded no_clear_difference because both printed intervals include zero, despite the authors' stronger narrative about reduced originality in rounds. The code_url is for the open-source intervention application, not confirmed analysis code or participant data: p. 4 cites La Scala (2024), whose p. 16 reference is Collaborative Ideation (Version 3.2.0), Zenodo.
